subject: Environmental Science
topic: Energy transfer, productivity and ecosystem models
scope: Original introductory ecology. Numerical examples are hypothetical and are not measurements from a real ecosystem or a complete AP/IB syllabus mapping.
prerequisites: Distinguish an organism from its environment.
Calculate percentages and read a simple flow diagram.
objectives: Distinguish energy flow from matter cycling.
Interpret food-web arrows and trophic transfer.
Calculate a stated transfer efficiency and evaluate model limits.

notes.heading: Energy enters and is transferred
paragraphs: An ecosystem includes organisms and their physical environment, connected through exchanges of matter and energy. In many ecosystems, producers capture light energy through photosynthesis and store some of it in chemical forms. Consumers obtain chemical energy by feeding, while decomposers use organic material from dead organisms and wastes. A food-chain arrow conventionally points from the food resource toward the organism receiving material and energy from it. Real feeding relationships usually form a web, because organisms may consume several resources and occupy different feeding roles over their lives.

notes.heading: Transfer is incomplete
paragraphs: Not all energy at one trophic level becomes biomass available to the next. Some material is not consumed, some consumed material is not assimilated, and assimilated energy supports respiration and other biological processes. Energy transferred to the surroundings as heat is not recycled into biological chemical energy by a closed trophic loop. Matter can be repeatedly exchanged through biogeochemical cycles, but ecosystems require continuing energy input. A fixed ten-percent rule is only a rough teaching approximation, not a universal efficiency for every organism, trophic link or ecosystem. Use the values and definitions supplied in the actual question.

notes.heading: Productivity and units
paragraphs: Productivity is a rate of biomass or energy production, so its units include time and often an area or volume. Gross primary productivity describes the total rate of energy fixation by producers under the chosen definition. Net primary productivity subtracts the producers' respiratory use from gross production. Do not confuse a standing biomass stock at one moment with the rate at which new biomass is produced. Comparisons need compatible units, periods and system boundaries. A number reported per square metre per year cannot be compared directly with a whole-region total without accounting for area and time.

notes.heading: Models, change and evidence
paragraphs: A food web helps predict possible pathways of influence, but a change in one population need not cause a single simple response everywhere else. Alternative foods, competition, seasonal changes and environmental conditions can modify the outcome. An energy pyramid concerns flows over a defined period; a biomass pyramid concerns a stock and can look different where producers turn over rapidly. Distinguish these quantities before interpreting a diagram. An ecological explanation should identify the proposed mechanism and the evidence needed to test it. Avoid treating a hypothetical numerical exercise as a measured account of an actual habitat, or a short-term observation as proof of a permanent ecosystem trend.

notes.heading: Comparing productivity over a common area and time
paragraphs: Energy-transfer comparisons need matching units and boundaries. A transfer percentage compares energy incorporated at the next trophic level with the energy available at the previous one over the same area and interval. Gross primary productivity includes the energy fixed by producers before their respiratory use is subtracted; net primary productivity is the remainder available for growth and other transfers. Not all net production is consumed by herbivores, and not all consumed energy becomes herbivore biomass. Keep these stages distinct rather than using one unexplained ten-percent rule. The example values are fictional and do not represent a measured ecosystem or a universal ecological constant.

notes.heading: Match the time interval before comparing stocks and flows
paragraphs: Standing biomass is the material present at a moment; productivity is the rate at which new biomass or stored chemical energy is produced. A small standing stock can support substantial annual production if it turns over rapidly. Transfers should use compatible areas, intervals and energy units, with the denominator named. Consumer ingestion, assimilation and production refer to different stages: not all ingested energy is assimilated, and some assimilated energy supports respiration. Numerical efficiency therefore depends on which stage is being compared, not merely on placing two available numbers into a percentage.

workedExamples.prompt: A producer level stores 2000 units of energy over a defined interval, and 150 reach the next level as new biomass. Calculate the stated transfer efficiency.
steps: Use energy received divided by energy available under the question's definition.
Keep both energy quantities within the same interval and boundary.

workedExamples.prompt: Gross primary productivity is 900 energy units per area per year and producer respiration is 350 in matching units. Find net primary productivity.
steps: Retain the rate and area units.
workedExamples.answer: 550 energy units per area per year.

workedExamples.prompt: Explain why a small producer biomass can support a larger consumer biomass at a particular moment in some aquatic systems.
steps: A biomass measurement is a standing stock, not a production rate.
Rapid producer growth and consumption can renew a small stock repeatedly.
The observation does not reverse the overall direction of energy transfer.
workedExamples.answer: Rapid turnover can produce an inverted standing-biomass pattern without an inverted energy-flow budget.

workedExamples.prompt: A fictional ecosystem has GPP of 18,000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and producer respiration of 7,500 in the same units. Herbivore production is 840. Find NPP and herbivore production as a percentage of NPP.
steps: Use NPP as the stated denominator: 840/10,500 × 100.
The result is 8%, with area and time units matched.
workedExamples.answer: NPP is 10,500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹; herbivore production is 8% of NPP.

misconceptions.claim: Energy cycles through an ecosystem in the same way as matter.
misconceptions.correction: Energy flows through transformations and is dissipated to the surroundings; continued input is needed.

misconceptions.claim: Every trophic transfer is exactly ten percent efficient.
misconceptions.correction: Efficiency varies; calculate from specified data rather than imposing a universal value.

flashcards.front: What does a food-web arrow from grass to an insect conventionally show?
flashcards.back: Transfer from the resource toward the consumer receiving material and energy.

flashcards.front: How is net primary productivity related to gross primary productivity?
flashcards.back: NPP equals GPP minus the producers' respiratory use, with matching units and definitions.

flashcards.front: How does biomass differ from productivity?
flashcards.back: Biomass is a stock at a time; productivity is a rate of production.

flashcards.front: How is a stated trophic transfer efficiency calculated?
flashcards.back: Energy transferred to the specified next level divided by the specified input, multiplied by 100%.

flashcards.front: Why does energy loss to the surroundings matter for ecosystem budgets?
flashcards.back: It reduces energy available for further biological transfer and requires continuing energy input.

flashcards.front: Why can a small standing producer stock still have high productivity?
flashcards.back: Rapid growth and replacement can generate substantial production over time despite a small instantaneous stock.

flashcards.front: How are gross and net primary productivity related?
flashcards.back: NPP = GPP minus producer respiration over the same area and time.

flashcards.front: Why is transfer efficiency not a universal ten percent?
flashcards.back: It depends on the organisms, pathways, conditions and the quantities used as numerator and denominator.

questions.prompt: Which quantity is a rate rather than a standing stock?
solution: A rate includes change or production over time.
Annual productivity measures production per time interval.
markingPoints: Select net primary productivity per year.

questions.prompt: A defined trophic transfer passes 120 energy units from an available 1600 units over the same interval. Find transfer efficiency as a percentage.
solution: Divide transferred energy by the stated available energy: 120/1600.
Multiply by 100 to express a percentage.

questions.prompt: Explain why an energy-flow value per hectare per year cannot be directly compared with a whole-forest annual total.
questions.answer: One value is normalised by area and the other is not. The forest area is needed to convert them to a common basis.
solution: Identify the different spatial denominators.
Convert using area before comparing like quantities.

questions.prompt: Explain why a decrease in one prey population does not guarantee that every predator in its food web declines immediately.
questions.answer: Predators may use alternative foods, differ in their dependence on that prey, or respond after a delay. A food-web link identifies a possible pathway, not a complete quantitative prediction under all conditions.
solution: Identify variation in dependence or alternative resources.
Consider timing or other environmental influences.
Limit the prediction to what the model supports.
markingPoints: Explain the limit of the deterministic claim.

questions.prompt: A learner interprets a biomass pyramid as an energy pyramid. Identify the conceptual error and two checks needed before drawing conclusions.
questions.answer: Biomass is an instantaneous stock, while energy-flow diagrams describe transfers over a period. Check the diagram's quantity and units, and check the time interval or turnover assumptions before interpreting trophic relationships.
solution: Distinguish stock from flow.
Inspect the quantity and units.
Identify the relevant time boundary or turnover information.

questions.prompt: A fictional ecosystem has GPP of 18,000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ and producer respiration of 7,500 in the same units. Herbivore production is 840. Find NPP and herbivore production as a percentage of NPP.
questions.answer: NPP is 10,500 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹; herbivore production is 8% of NPP.
solution: Subtract producer respiration from GPP: 18,000 - 7,500 = 10,500.
Use NPP as the stated denominator: 840/10,500 × 100.
The result is 8%, with area and time units matched.
markingPoints: Use NPP as the stated denominator: 840/10,500 × 100.
The result is 8%, with area and time units matched.

questions.prompt: A learner says the remaining 92% of NPP was all destroyed. Explain two reasons this interpretation is wrong.
questions.answer: Energy is transferred, not destroyed; some NPP is not eaten by herbivores, and some consumed energy is transferred through respiration or waste rather than new biomass.
solution: Conservation of energy rules out destruction as the explanation.
Uneaten plant material can enter other pathways such as detrital food webs.
Consumed energy can be transferred as heat through respiration or leave in waste rather than herbivore production.
markingPoints: Conservation of energy rules out destruction as the explanation.
Uneaten plant material can enter other pathways such as detrital food webs.
Consumed energy can be transferred as heat through respiration or leave in waste rather than herbivore production.

questions.prompt: In an invented ecosystem, producer biomass is 20 g m⁻² and annual production is 200 g m⁻² year⁻¹. Consumer biomass is 30 g m⁻² and production is 60 g m⁻² year⁻¹. Explain why an inverted biomass comparison need not imply inverted production.
questions.answer: Consumers have more standing biomass, 30 versus 20, but producers have greater annual production, 200 versus 60. Producer production/biomass is 10 per year versus 2 per year for consumers.
solution: Separate stock units from production-rate units.
Compute turnover ratios to explain how a small producer stock can support substantial flow.
markingPoints: Compare production in the opposite order.
Use turnover ratios 10 and 2 per year.

questions.prompt: A fictional consumer ingests 1,000 kJ, loses 300 kJ in unassimilated material and uses 500 kJ in respiration during a defined interval. Assuming these are the only losses, find assimilation and production.
questions.answer: Assimilation is 700 kJ and production is 200 kJ.
solution: Subtract unassimilated material from ingestion.
Subtract respiration from assimilation under the stated budget.

questions.prompt: Plot A produces 6,000 kJ m⁻² year⁻¹ over 2 hectares; plot B produces 90,000,000 kJ per year in total. Using 1 hectare=10,000 m², compare total annual production and explain what is missing for a per-area comparison.
questions.answer: A totals 120,000,000 kJ per year, exceeding B by 30,000,000. B's area is needed to compare production per unit area.
solution: Convert A's 2 hectares to 20,000 m².
Multiply its areal rate by area, then distinguish total from areal comparison.
markingPoints: Require B's area for a per-area comparison.

revisionChecklist: State the system boundary and units.
Distinguish stocks, rates and transfer efficiencies.
Explain mechanisms without treating a simple web as a complete forecast.
Explain the reasoning in “Separate productivity stages” and correct the linked error-analysis response without copying its solution.
